## Why Fabric Weight Is the Most Important Decision in Lace Hijab Production

When buyers ask us about modal lace hijabs, the first question we ask back is: what weight do you want? It sounds technical, but the answer determines everything 鈥?whether the lace lies flat, whether the scarf drapes with the right fluidity, and whether the final piece holds up after washing.

After producing lace-edge scarves for buyers in the United Kingdom, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia and the United States since 2008, we have settled on a **finished scarf weight of 100鈥?20 g/m虏** as the only range that works reliably with a sewn lace trim. The modal base fabric itself weighs 60鈥?0 g/m虏; the lace trim adds a further 20鈥?0 g/m虏 concentrated along the long edges, bringing the finished piece into the 100鈥?20 g/m虏 range.

### The Physics of Lace Attachment

Lace trim is attached along the long edges of the scarf using a header tape that is stitched through both layers. At weights **below 100 g/m虏**, the base fabric does not have enough body to support the weight of the header tape. The result is a wavy, puckering edge that is difficult to press flat even with a steam iron. At weights **above 120 g/m虏**, the fabric loses the soft drape that is the defining quality of modal 鈥?it begins to feel like a structured woven rather than a knit, and the lace trim can appear rigid.

At a **finished weight of approximately 110 g/m虏** (60鈥?0 g/m虏 modal base plus 40鈥?0 g/m虏 lace trim contribution), the scarf falls naturally from the shoulder, the lace header tape lies flat without intervention, and the finished piece presses cleanly for retail packaging.

### Our First-Pass Yield Target: 95鈥?8%

In factory quality language, first-pass yield (FPY) is the percentage of units that pass inspection without any rework. For a lace hijab, the inspection points are:

1. **Lace alignment** 鈥?the lace pattern repeat must be continuous across each long edge, with no visible join offset
2. **Hem tension** 鈥?the lace edge must not pull the fabric off-grain when laid flat
3. **Colour match** 鈥?the lace colour is matched against a Pantone reference card; tolerance is 螖E 鈮?2.0

Our current FPY for modal lace hijabs is **95鈥?8%**. The 2鈥?% that require rework are almost always hem-tension issues caught at the ironing station before packaging. No unit leaves our floor with a failed lace-alignment check.

### Size Preferences by Market

| Market | Preferred size | Notes |

| United Kingdom | 185 脳 75 cm | Buyers prefer a slightly longer drape |
| Gulf (UAE, Saudi Arabia) | 190 脳 80 cm | Wider width for layered styling |
| Malaysia & Indonesia | 175 脳 65 cm | Lighter feel, easier to pin |
| United States | 180 脳 70 cm | Standard export; occasionally 185 脳 70 cm |
| Germany / France | 180 脳 70 cm | Standard; some requests for 185 脳 75 cm |

We also produce **children's lace scarves** at 120鈥?40 脳 55 cm, which are popular for school-uniform programmes in Malaysia and the UK.

### Custom from 1 Piece 鈥?Our Small-Batch Programme

Traditional hijab manufacturing operates on minimum orders of 300鈥?00 pieces per colour. That model made sense when printing and cut-and-sew were separate facilities. We have restructured our workflow so that:

- **Cut**: we cut fabric in single-piece increments from our continuously running modal stock
- **Trim**: lace is attached on our finishing machines in any quantity
- **Pack**: each piece is inspected to the same FPY standard regardless of order size

The result is that **a buyer can order one lace hijab in a custom colour and custom size**, receive it in 5 days as a sample, and then scale to bulk production with the same specification locked in.

This is particularly valuable for:
- New brands ordering one sample before committing to bulk
- Retailers testing a colourway with a small run before the main season
- Buyers who need a specific size not available from stock (children's, plus-size, extended length)

## The Engineering Behind a Ruffle Hijab That Keeps Its Shape

A ruffle hijab looks simple 鈥?fabric gathered into waves along the sides of a scarf. In practice it is one of the most fabric-sensitive products we manufacture. The ruffles must cascade freely, return to shape after washing, and not collapse under their own weight by mid-afternoon.

The variable that determines all three outcomes is fabric weight.

### Why Finished Ruffle Scarves Target 100鈥?20 g/m虏

Ruffles work by gathering a wider strip of fabric onto a shorter edge. The ratio of the strip width to the finished edge length is the gather ratio 鈥?we typically run at 2:1 to 2.5:1. At this ratio, the fabric loops back on itself and the spring of the loops is what gives the ruffle its visible volume.

At **below 100 g/m虏**, the fabric has too little spring. The ruffles flatten against the body within a few minutes of wearing. The gather ratio needs to increase to 3:1 or above to compensate, which adds significant fabric cost and makes the ruffle heavy and bunched at the attachment point.

At **above 120 g/m虏**, the fabric becomes too stiff to gather smoothly. The ruffles form angular folds rather than soft curves, and the attachment seam is visible as a hard line.

At a **finished weight of 100鈥?20 g/m虏** (60鈥?0 g/m虏 modal base plus 20鈥?0 g/m虏 from the bias-cut ruffle strips) the loops hold their cylindrical shape, the attachment seam is hidden by the natural fold of the first layer, and the scarf washes and dries without requiring steaming.

### Bias Cutting and Its Effect on Yield

We cut ruffle strips on the bias 鈥?at 45 degrees to the fabric grain 鈥?rather than on the straight grain. Bias-cut fabric stretches and recovers in a way that helps the ruffle maintain its shape without stiffening or fraying at the edge.

The trade-off is waste. Bias cutting produces more offcuts than straight-grain cutting because the strips are diagonal across the fabric roll. We recover approximately 78% of the modal fabric per roll on ruffle production, compared to 88% on plain straight-cut scarves.

Against this, bias-cut ruffles contribute to our **95鈥?8% first-pass yield** on the finished scarf. Our inspection points are:

- **Gathering uniformity**: ruffle density must be consistent within 卤15% along the full length
- **Layer separation**: each tier must be visually distinct when the scarf is held at arm's length
- **Attachment tension**: the ruffle must lie flat against the scarf body without pulling the fabric off-grain

Units that fail gathering uniformity are the most common rework 鈥?typically caused by a tension variation on the gathering foot at the start or end of a run.

### Size Preferences by Market: What the Data Tells Us

Over 18 years of exporting ruffle hijabs, we have collected a clear picture of how market preferences differ:

| Market | Preferred size | Ruffle style notes |
|---|---|---|
| Gulf (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait) | 190 脳 80 cm | Prefer 3 tiers with deep 10鈥?2 cm layers |

| Germany | 180 脳 70 cm | Standard; occasionally 3-tier with single ruffle side |

We also produce **children's ruffle scarves** at 130 脳 55 cm, typically ordered by Gulf buyers for girls' school uniforms.

## What Buyers Don't Know About Tassel Hijab Production (But Should)

Tassel fringe looks like a simple finishing detail. It is, in fact, the most labour-intensive part of a modal hijab and the element most likely to cause a failed shipment if the specification is not defined precisely.

The three variables that matter most to wholesale buyers are: **fringe length**, **knot density**, and **header tension**. None of these is visible from a product photograph, which is why we publish this data for buyers who are evaluating suppliers.

### Fringe Length: The Market Splits at 6 cm

After analysing orders from 50+ countries, we see a consistent split in tassel length preference:

| Market | Preferred tassel length | Styling context |
|---|---|---|
| Malaysia, Indonesia | 5 cm | Shorter fringe for school and office wear |
| Singapore | 5鈥? cm | Conservative styling; long fringe considered impractical |
| Gulf (UAE, Saudi Arabia) | 6鈥? cm | Moderate length; longer fringe on occasion wear |
| Turkey | 6鈥? cm | Often with braided header band |
| United Kingdom | 8鈥?0 cm | Fashion-forward buyers prefer longer, swing fringe |
| Germany, France | 8鈥?0 cm | Statement accessory market |
| United States | 8鈥?2 cm | Bohemian and festival markets push to 12 cm |

Our default production length is **8 cm**, which is acceptable in all markets. Buyers with a specific preference should state the length at order placement 鈥?retrimming after production is possible but adds 2鈥? days.

### Knot Density: Why 28 Tassels per 10 cm Is Our Minimum

Tassel fringe is knotted onto a woven header band. The density of the knots determines how the fringe falls: sparse fringe (below 20 tassels per 10 cm) falls in visible gaps; dense fringe (28+ per 10 cm) falls as a continuous curtain.

We set our minimum at **28 tassels per 10 cm** because below this threshold the fringe parts when the scarf moves, revealing the header band. Above 36 per 10 cm the header band bunches and the fringe is difficult to straighten after packaging.

The knots are tied by hand. Each operator produces approximately 300 tassels per hour, which means a full 180 cm scarf (two short edges 脳 70 cm each = 140 cm of fringe) requires approximately 45 minutes of hand-knotting time per unit.

### Yield at 95鈥?8%: What Goes Wrong

Our first-pass yield target for tassel hijabs is **95鈥?8%**. The failure modes are:

1. **Loose knot** (most common): the tassel slips through the header band loop. Caught at the pre-pack tug test; unit returned for re-knotting.
2. **Colour bleed** (rare): tassel thread and base fabric dyed in separate batches can show a slight colour difference under strong light. We batch-match all orders to keep 螖E 鈮?2.0.
3. **Density gap**: a section of the header band has fewer than 28 tassels per 10 cm. Caught at the density ruler check; unit returned for infill.

Buyers should request our inspection report with each shipment 鈥?it states the FPY for that batch, the failure category, and the count of reworked units.

### The 100鈥?20 g/m虏 Finished Weight Requirement for Tassel Hijabs

Modal base fabric weighs 60鈥?0 g/m虏. For tassel hijabs, the hand-knotted header band and fringe add approximately 20鈥?0 g/m虏 across the finished piece (concentrated at the short edges), bringing the finished scarf to 100鈥?20 g/m虏 total. At finished weights **below 100 g/m虏**, the short ends hang lower than the body of the scarf, creating an uneven drape. At the **100鈥?20 g/m虏 finished range**, the fabric body is sufficient to balance the header weight and the scarf hangs with a consistent fall.

## How Computer Embroidery Meets Hand-Inspection: Inside Floral-Trim Hijab Production

Embroidered floral trim is the most technically precise of the four craft finishes we produce. Unlike lace (which is a separate fabric attached by tape) or ruffles (which use the base fabric), embroidered trim is stitched directly onto the selvedge of the modal fabric 鈥?meaning any colour registration error is permanent and cannot be corrected without cutting the entire edge.

This is why our production process for floral-trim hijabs is structured around prevention rather than rework.

### The Embroidery Process: Computer-Stitched, Hand-Inspected

Each floral motif is programmed into our embroidery machines as a digital file. The machine stitches the motif sequence continuously along the fabric edge at a rate of approximately 800 stitches per minute. A 180 cm scarf edge requires roughly 12鈥?5 minutes of machine time per side.

After machine embroidery, each piece passes through a manual inspection where the inspector checks:

1. **Registration accuracy**: the first and last motif in the sequence must align with the fabric selvedge to within 卤1 mm. A deviation greater than 1 mm is visible to the naked eye.
2. **Thread tension**: loose thread loops indicate a tension fault on the machine. These pieces are rejected and the machine is re-tensioned before the run continues.
3. **Colour accuracy**: the embroidery thread colour is matched against a Pantone reference. Our tolerance is 螖E 鈮?1.5 鈥?tighter than our lace or tassel specifications because the embroidery contrast against the base fabric makes colour difference more visible.

This three-point inspection process is how we achieve **95鈥?8% first-pass yield** on floral-trim hijabs. The 2鈥?% that require rework are almost entirely tension faults, which are caught at the thread-loop check before the scarf is pressed.

### Trim Width: 1.5 cm to 3 cm

The default trim width we produce is **2 cm**, which is wide enough to be clearly visible in retail photography and narrow enough to feel refined rather than decorative. Buyers can specify any width between 1.5 cm and 3 cm at order placement.

We do not produce trim wider than 3 cm on modal fabric because wider embroidery strips add significant weight to the selvedge, causing the scarf to hang unevenly when worn. If a buyer requires a wider border, we recommend using a separate lace or woven trim rather than direct embroidery.

### Size Preferences: How UK and Malaysian Buyers Differ

| Saudi Arabia, UAE | 190 脳 80 cm | 2鈥? cm; prefers gold thread motifs |
| United States | 180 脳 70 cm | 2 cm; multi-colour floral popular |

The UK preference for a larger scarf reflects a styling choice 鈥?UK buyers tend to drape the scarf more loosely, requiring extra length and width. The Malaysian preference for a smaller, lighter scarf reflects climate and pinning style.

We also produce **children's floral-trim scarves** at 120鈥?40 脳 55 cm, which are popular for school uniform programmes and Eid gifting in Malaysia and the Gulf.

### The 100鈥?20 g/m虏 Finished Weight Requirement

For floral-trim hijabs, the computer-stitched embroidery adds approximately 20鈥?0 g/m虏 concentrated along the selvedge, bringing the finished scarf to 100鈥?20 g/m虏 total. At the **100鈥?20 g/m虏 finished range**, the fabric body is sufficient to absorb the thread weight without distortion.

body:
## The Problem Most Hijab Brands Encounter at the Qualification Stage

A DTC hijab brand in London or Los Angeles faces a specific problem when evaluating manufacturers: almost every factory in Yiwu or Keqiao presents nearly identical capability claims. The catalogue shows printed modal and jersey hijabs; the price list is competitive; the minimum order quantity is stated. What is not shown is how the factory performs when something goes wrong 鈥?when the modal base absorbs more dye than expected, when the jersey stretches during printing, or when a seasonal colour needs to be matched precisely across three production batches.

The brands that build reliable supply chains are the ones that move past catalogue evaluation and into process-level qualification. This article describes the exact criteria those brands use, and what a factory needs to demonstrate at each step.

---

## Section 1: What European and US DTC Brands Are Actually Looking For in 2026

The modest fashion market in Europe and the United States has become significantly more segmented over the past three years. Instagram and TikTok brands are not competing on price 鈥?they are competing on **visual distinctiveness and fabric feel**. A hijab that photographs well in a studio setting and feels different from a competitor's product in hand is the basis of a premium position.

This has shifted what qualified buyers ask manufacturers:

**Visual distinctiveness** requires print quality that holds across orders. A brand that launches a floral-print modal collection needs the second production run to look identical to the first. Colour delta-E variation of more than 2.0 between batches is visible to consumers in side-by-side social media comparisons, which is where most purchasing decisions are made.

**Fabric feel** requires GSM consistency. A 65 g/m虏 modal base drapes differently from a 72 g/m虏 modal base of the same composition. Brands that have built their product positioning around "the lightest hijab for summer" or "structured enough to hold a fold without pinning" need a factory that holds base weight within a 卤3 g/m虏 tolerance across orders.

**Reliability at small quantities** is the third factor. A brand doing 500鈥?,500 units per design run cannot absorb the yield loss that comes from a factory with inconsistent QC. Each defective unit at that scale represents a meaningful percentage of the total order.

---

## Section 2: The Qualification Questions That Reveal Process Quality

When a DTC or private label brand contacts a factory, the initial conversation is usually about price and minimum order quantity. The brands that consistently find good suppliers ask a second set of questions within the first week of contact:

**"Can you show me your first-pass yield data for printed modal?"**

First-pass yield (FPY) is the percentage of units that pass the full quality inspection on the first attempt, without rework. A factory that tracks this number has a formalised QC process. A factory that cannot answer the question is running visual spot-check QC, which produces inconsistent results.

For printed modal hijabs, an FPY of 95鈥?8% means that for every 1,000 units produced, 20鈥?0 require rework (typically a colour touch, re-hem, or reprint of a specific section). An FPY below 90% means systematic process problems 鈥?usually in colour consistency or GSM variation 鈥?that will surface in the bulk order.

**"What is your colour delta-E tolerance, and how do you enforce it?"**

Delta-E is the standard measurement of colour difference. A delta-E of 1.0 is barely perceptible to a trained eye. Delta-E of 2.0 is visible under direct comparison. Delta-E of 3.5 is clearly visible in standard lighting.

A factory that enforces colour accuracy will have a defined tolerance (typically 螖E 鈮?2.0 for branded production runs) and will own a spectrophotometer to measure it. Factories that describe colour matching as "we match to your swatch" without a stated measurement standard are operating on subjective visual inspection.

**"What GSM tolerance do you hold on the base fabric?"**

The correct answer for premium production is 卤3 g/m虏 from the specified base weight. A 65 g/m虏 modal with a 卤3 g/m虏 tolerance means any unit in the order will fall between 62 and 68 g/m虏 鈥?a range that is perceptible in the hand but within brand standards. A factory that cannot state a tolerance cannot guarantee consistency.

---

## Section 3: Why Printed Modal and Jersey Present Different Manufacturing Challenges

Modal and jersey are not interchangeable substrates from a printing perspective. Brands sourcing both for their line need to understand why, and what it means for supplier selection.

**Printed modal** presents a **dye absorption challenge**. Modal fibre is more hydrophilic than polyester 鈥?it absorbs water, including the aqueous dye solutions used in reactive and digital printing, faster and more unevenly than a standard woven fabric. The result, in a factory with uncalibrated equipment, is dye bleeding and colour graduation (a darkening at one end of the print relative to the other). Solving this requires adjusting the pre-treatment moisture content and the print head pass speed for modal specifically 鈥?neither of which is the factory default setting for general textile printing.

**Printed jersey** presents a **stretch-during-printing challenge**. Jersey is a knit fabric with significant four-way stretch. As it passes through a printing machine under tension, it elongates. When the tension releases, the print contracts, compressing the artwork horizontally or vertically depending on the direction of elongation. The visible result is print distortion 鈥?a geometric pattern that should be square becomes slightly trapezoidal, or a face in a floral motif becomes compressed.

A factory that has solved both problems will describe their process differently from one that has not. They will specify their **fabric tension calibration procedure**, their **pre-treatment formulation for modal**, and their **print head height adjustment for jersey pile**. These are not generic answers; they are answers that can only come from having encountered and resolved the problem.

---

## Section 4: The Production Workflow That Produces Consistent Printed Hijabs

The production of a printed modal or jersey hijab involves more steps than a plain-fabric scarf, and each step is a potential source of variation.

**Step 1 鈥?Fabric inspection (pre-production)**
Rolls are checked against the purchase specification: composition, GSM, width tolerance, tensile strength. Any roll that fails is quarantined before it enters production. This step is skipped by factories treating fabric as a commodity input.

**Step 2 鈥?Pre-treatment**
Modal requires a pre-treatment coating that controls the rate of dye absorption. The formulation varies by dye type (reactive vs. digital ink) and by the specific modal blend being used. An incorrect pre-treatment produces uneven dye penetration 鈥?visible as patchy colour or unintended colour gradation.

**Step 3 鈥?Print calibration**
Before a production run begins, the printing equipment is calibrated against the target colour profile. This involves printing a test swatch, measuring it with a spectrophotometer, and adjusting ink density curves until the measurement falls within 螖E 1.5 of the target. Only then does production begin.

**Step 4 鈥?In-line colour checks**
During a production run, spot checks are performed at defined intervals 鈥?typically every 50 metres of fabric for a continuous print, and at each colour transition for a panel print. Units that fall outside 螖E 2.0 are pulled and reviewed before the run continues.

**Step 5 鈥?Cutting and hemming**
Hijabs are cut to the specified size from the printed roll. Edge finishing 鈥?rolled hem, overlocked edge, or trim attachment 鈥?is applied at this stage. Size variation should not exceed 卤1 cm in length and 卤0.5 cm in width from the stated specification.

**Step 6 鈥?Final inspection and packing**
Each unit is inspected against five criteria: colour match (spectrophotometer measurement), print clarity (magnified check at pattern join points), hem quality (tension and stitch evenness), size (tape measure check on a sample basis), and fabric integrity (no snags, pulls, or composition faults). Passed units are folded to a consistent dimension and packed to the brand specification.

---

## Section 5: How to Evaluate a Factory Before Placing a Bulk Order

The most reliable evaluation method for a DTC or private label brand is a **structured sample order** rather than a generic sample request.

A structured sample order specifies:
- The exact base fabric composition and GSM target
- The print artwork in its final form (not a low-resolution reference)
- The target colour in Pantone references, not just "similar to the reference image"
- The finished size and hem style
- The packaging requirement

A factory that can produce a sample matching this specification, and that delivers it with a production record showing the calibration data used, has demonstrated the process capability needed for bulk production. A factory that delivers a visually acceptable sample without accompanying process data has demonstrated luck, not capability.

The sample lead time for a printed modal or jersey hijab should be 5鈥? working days from artwork confirmation. Significantly shorter suggests the sample was pulled from stock; significantly longer suggests the factory does not maintain a standing production setup for the fabric type.

After the sample, request a **production audit checklist** 鈥?a document that shows the QC checkpoints applied at each stage of production. This document will immediately distinguish factories with formalised QC from those operating on visual inspection.

---

## Section 6: Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best fabric for premium hijab brands?**

For printed hijabs, 95% modal with 5% spandex at 60鈥?0 g/m虏 base weight is the fabric most consistently requested by European and US premium brands. It delivers the drape, breathability, and colour saturation that digital and reactive printing require. Printed jersey (88% polyester, 12% spandex at 80鈥?00 g/m虏 base) is the second choice for performance and sport-hijab lines where stretch recovery and moisture-wicking take priority over drape. The two are not interchangeable; a supplier capable of both should be able to explain the specific process differences, not just list both on a catalogue.

**How can brands customise printed hijabs?**

Brands can customise the base fabric colour, print artwork (AI / PSD / high-resolution TIFF format), finished size (standard 180脳70 cm or any custom dimension, including children's scarves), edge trim (lace, ruffle, tassel fringe, or embroidered floral border), and retail packaging (woven labels, hang-tags, tissue paper, poly bag). A factory with small-batch production capability can accommodate single-piece samples for each variation before a bulk commitment. Custom Pantone colour matching is standard for established printed-hijab manufacturers; any factory that cannot describe their colour-matching measurement process should be treated as a risk.

**What should buyers check before choosing a hijab supplier?**

Request first-pass yield data for the specific product type (printed modal or printed jersey). Ask for the factory's stated GSM tolerance and colour delta-E tolerance, and ask how those tolerances are enforced 鈥?what measuring equipment they use and at what intervals. Send your own print artwork and receive a sample produced from it, not a pre-existing sample pulled from stock. Review the sample against your specification with your own measuring tools before approving. A factory that produces a correct sample consistently across two or three iterations, and that can show process documentation for each, is operating at a level appropriate for branded production.

## The Question Every Hijab Brand Faces When Building a New Collection

When a DTC or private-label hijab brand begins developing a new seasonal collection, one decision determines almost everything else about the product: modal or jersey. The two fabrics look similar in a catalogue, often arrive at comparable prices, and are both described by manufacturers as "soft, breathable, and suitable for hijab production."

They are not interchangeable. The choice between printed modal and printed jersey determines how the fabric drapes when worn, how the print looks under natural light versus studio lighting, how the hijab behaves after 30 wash cycles, and which printing process the manufacturer needs to use. Brands that understand the difference before placing a sample order avoid the most common sourcing mistake in the hijab category: approving a sample that looks correct but fails in the customer's hands six months later.

This guide compares the two fabrics from a manufacturing perspective, using the specific parameters that experienced buyers check before committing to a production run.

---

## Section 1: Why the Modal vs. Jersey Decision Has Become More Consequential

Three years ago, most European and US hijab brands operated in one of two categories: luxury silk or occasion scarves at the high end, and basic jersey or chiffon at the accessible end. The middle ground 鈥?premium everyday hijabs with distinctive prints, presented through editorial photography 鈥?was underdeveloped.

That middle ground is now the fastest-growing segment of the market. Instagram and TikTok brands have built audiences around product photography in which fabric quality is visible frame by frame. A hijab that reads as "flat" or "synthetic" in a photo 鈥?regardless of how it feels 鈥?loses the visual competition before a buyer clicks through.

This shift has made fabric selection a brand strategy decision, not just a procurement one. Printed modal and printed jersey serve different visual identities, different customer use cases, and different brand narratives. The manufacturer that can produce both to a consistent standard is able to support a brand as its line expands; a manufacturer calibrated for only one creates a constraint the brand will eventually outgrow.

---

## Section 2: What Buyers Need to Understand About Each Fabric Before Ordering

### What makes printed modal behave the way it does?

Printed modal starts from a fibre. Modal is a type of regenerated cellulose 鈥?produced from beech wood pulp through a wet-spinning process. The resulting fibre is more hydrophilic than cotton and significantly more hydrophilic than polyester. It absorbs moisture, including dye solutions, quickly and deeply.

The base fabric for a premium printed modal hijab runs at 60鈥?0 g/m虏 in the greige state. After digital or reactive printing, pre-treatment, and finishing, the finished scarf reaches approximately 100鈥?20 g/m虏 depending on the trim applied. This weight range produces the characteristic drape of a modal hijab: the fabric falls from the shoulder in a continuous, unbroken line without the bulk of heavier wovens or the stiffness of synthetic knits.

The trade-off is print complexity. Because modal absorbs dye aggressively, printing on it requires tighter control of pre-treatment moisture content and ink density than printing on polyester. A factory that prints modal using settings calibrated for chiffon or standard cotton will produce results with uneven dye penetration 鈥?visible as colour gradation (darker at one end of the scarf than the other) or bleeding at fine-line print details.

### What makes printed jersey behave differently?

Printed jersey uses a polyester-dominant base 鈥?typically 88% polyester, 12% spandex 鈥?at 80鈥?00 g/m虏 in the greige state. Polyester does not absorb dye in the same way as modal; it requires sublimation printing (where dye is converted to gas and bonded to the polymer structure under heat) or, for reactive-type effects, a specialised pre-treatment followed by digital printing.

The finished jersey hijab has different physical properties from modal. Four-way stretch means the fabric moves with the wearer rather than draping away from the body. Moisture-wicking keeps the inner surface dry. UPF 40+ protection is achievable with standard polyester constructions without additional finishing 鈥?the fibre structure itself blocks UV radiation.

The printing challenge for jersey is dimensional: jersey knit stretches under tension. A fabric roll fed through a printing machine under standard tension will be elongated at the point of printing, then return to its original dimensions when tension is released. The print contracts with it, and a geometric repeat that was designed as a 10脳10 cm square becomes approximately 9.5脳10.5 cm in the finished product. This is invisible in most floral or abstract prints but immediately apparent in geometric, typographic, or repeat-pattern designs.

---

## Section 3: How an Experienced Factory Handles the Technical Differences

A manufacturer that produces both printed modal and printed jersey under one production system 鈥?without separate calibration for each 鈥?is producing both at a compromise. The settings that work for modal pre-treatment will produce under-bonded dye on jersey; the tension controls that produce accurate pattern registration on jersey will produce bleed on modal.

The correct approach separates the two into distinct process streams:

**For printed modal:**

Pre-treatment with a moisture-buffering agent is applied before printing to moderate the dye absorption rate. The digital print head height is set for the pile height of the knit, not for a flat woven. Ink density curves are calibrated for modal's absorption characteristics using a test print, measured with a spectrophotometer at 螖E 鈮?2.0 before the production run begins. In-line colour checks are performed every 50 metres.

**For printed jersey:**

Fabric tension during feed is monitored and compensated. The print artwork is pre-distorted in the RIP software to account for the 3鈥?% elongation characteristic of the specific jersey construction being used 鈥?this pre-distortion means the final print, after tension release, matches the original artwork dimensions. Sublimation fixation temperature and dwell time are calibrated for the spandex content, because spandex begins to degrade above 200掳C and most polyester sublimation processes run at 180鈥?95掳C.

These are not interchangeable production settings. They require different pre-treatment chemistry, different equipment parameters, and different quality checkpoints.

---

## Section 4: Reading the Visual Difference in Photography and in the Hand

Understanding the technical differences matters for sourcing, but the brand ultimately makes the fabric decision based on what the product looks and feels like to their customer.

**In photography**, printed modal reads with a soft, matte surface that absorbs light rather than reflecting it. The result is a fabric that looks refined and expensive in natural-light editorial photography 鈥?the surface holds shadow and highlight well, giving the fabric dimension without appearing shiny. This is why modal is the fabric of choice for brands whose aesthetic references luxury fashion editorials.

Printed jersey in photography has a subtle sheen from the polyester content. Under ring-light or studio lighting, this sheen is immediately visible and can read as synthetic if the print design or styling does not account for it. Under natural light in outdoor photography, jersey's sheen is less apparent and the four-way stretch means the fabric moves naturally on the model, which reads well in video content.

**In the hand**, modal has a warmth and softness that polyester does not replicate. Consumers who have worn quality modal describe it as "similar to a fine cotton T-shirt, but lighter." Jersey has a different hand 鈥?cooler, more functional, with a spring-back when stretched. For an active or sport-hijab customer, this is a positive quality. For a customer buying an everyday premium hijab, it can feel less luxurious than modal at the same price point.

---

## Section 5: Which Fabric Profile Matches Which Brand

Brands that have worked through this decision across multiple collections tend to arrive at the same framework:

**Printed modal is the correct choice when:**
- The brand's visual identity is editorial, lifestyle, or fashion-forward
- The primary use case is everyday wear or occasions where drape matters
- The collection is photographed predominantly in natural light
- The customer profile values fabric feel as a purchase driver

**Printed jersey is the correct choice when:**
- The brand is building a sport, active, or performance hijab line
- The customer engages in activities 鈥?running, gym, swimming, cycling 鈥?where moisture management and stretch recovery are functional requirements
- The brand is targeting markets (Gulf, Southeast Asia, UK sports retail) where performance hijabs are a recognised category
- UPF protection is a stated product feature

**Both fabrics in parallel is viable when:**
- The brand runs a main collection (modal, lifestyle-focused) and a sport sub-line (jersey, performance-focused) under one brand identity
- The manufacturer produces both under one roof with separate calibration, so seasonal colours can be matched across the two fabric types without visible discrepancy

A manufacturer capable of producing both to the same colour fidelity standard (螖E 鈮?2.0) is able to support a brand expanding from one fabric type to two without sourcing a second supplier.

---

## Section 6: Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best fabric for premium hijab brands?**

The answer depends on the brand's product position. Printed modal (95% modal, 5% spandex, 60鈥?0 g/m虏 base weight, finished at 100鈥?20 g/m虏) is the fabric most consistently requested by lifestyle and everyday-luxury brands 鈥?it drapes softly, photographs with a matte depth, and takes reactive and digital print with high colour fidelity. Printed jersey (88% polyester, 12% spandex, 80鈥?00 g/m虏 base) is the correct fabric for sport and performance lines where four-way stretch, moisture-wicking, and UPF 40+ protection are functional requirements rather than optional features. Neither is universally superior; the question is which properties serve the brand's specific customer.

**How can brands customise printed hijabs in modal or jersey?**

Both fabrics support full specification control: base colour (Pantone reference or physical swatch match), print artwork (AI, PSD, or high-resolution TIFF files accepted), finished size (standard 180脳70 cm, or any custom dimension from children's scarves at 120脳55 cm to extended lengths above 200 cm), and edge finishing (rolled hem, lace trim, ruffle, tassel fringe, or embroidered border). Sampling is available from 1 piece. A single-piece sample should be produced from the buyer's actual print artwork and target specifications, not from a pre-existing stock design 鈥?the sample's purpose is to validate the specific combination of fabric, print, and size, not to confirm the factory's general capability.

**What should buyers check before choosing a hijab fabric supplier?**

Ask whether the factory has separate process calibration for modal and jersey 鈥?not whether they produce both, but whether the pre-treatment, tension control, and print parameters are differentiated between the two substrates. Request first-pass yield data: the target range for a manufacturer with systematic quality control is 95鈥?8% across both fabric types. Specify your target GSM and ask for a spec sheet showing their tolerance (卤3 g/m虏 is the standard). Confirm colour consistency standards: 螖E 鈮?2.0 between production batches is achievable with calibrated equipment and is the standard required for seasonal colour matching across a brand's collection.

## Why Colour Fastness Is the Test That Separates Good Samples from Reliable Production

A printed hijab can look correct on the day it arrives. The brand owner approves the sample, places the bulk order, and receives shipment six weeks later. The hijabs sell. Then the first wave of returns arrives: customers reporting that the print has faded after three washes, or that the colours have shifted to a different hue.

This is the most common post-shipment problem in the printed hijab category, and it is almost entirely preventable. The failure is not the colour 鈥?it is the absence of wash fastness verification before bulk production was approved.

Colour fastness testing tells a brand whether the dye applied to a fabric will remain stable under the conditions the end customer will actually expose it to: washing, rubbing, light exposure, and perspiration. The test results are standardised across international markets, which means a European brand and a US brand can specify the same minimum rating and know they are requiring the same standard.

This guide explains the tests, what the ratings mean, and what a brand should specifically ask their manufacturer to provide before releasing payment for bulk production.

---

## Section 1: The Market Pressure That Makes Colour Fastness More Important Than It Was Five Years Ago

Three developments in the European and US modest fashion market have made colour fastness a higher-stakes specification than it was for previous generations of wholesale buyers.

**Social media review velocity.** A customer who receives a faded hijab after two washes will post about it. The review appears publicly within hours and accumulates engagement 鈥?particularly on TikTok, where "disappointing quality" videos reach audiences far beyond the original follower base. A single quality failure that would previously have generated a few negative emails now generates searchable content that affects future purchase decisions.

**The premium price point creates a higher expectation.** Brands operating in the mid-to-premium segment 鈥?typically pricing hijabs at USD 35鈥?0 retail 鈥?attract customers who are comparing their product to established modest fashion labels. Those customers expect wash durability equivalent to a premium European jersey or a high-street modal scarf. When a product fails that expectation, the brand's positioning is damaged, not just the individual sale.

**Repeat purchase economics.** A DTC hijab brand's business model depends on repeat purchase rates. A customer who buys once and experiences colour fade has a low probability of returning. The acquisition cost of replacing that customer 鈥?through paid social, influencer seeding, or promotion 鈥?is typically three to five times the margin on the original sale. Colour fastness is not a quality-control detail; it is a customer lifetime value issue.

---

## Section 2: What Colour Fastness Tests Actually Measure

Colour fastness is not a single test. It is a family of tests, each measuring stability under a different type of stress. Brands and manufacturers reference several specific standards; understanding which tests matter for hijabs avoids the common mistake of requesting a test that does not reflect actual end-use conditions.

**ISO 105-C06: Colour Fastness to Domestic and Commercial Laundering**

This is the primary test for any garment that will be machine or hand washed. For hijabs, the relevant wash programme is typically A1S or A2S (30掳C or 40掳C, with a standard detergent), corresponding to the temperatures most hijab wearers use. The test exposes the fabric to the specified wash conditions and then rates colour change on a grey scale from 1 (severe change) to 5 (no perceptible change).

For a printed modal or printed jersey hijab sold to the European or US market, a minimum rating of 4 on ISO 105-C06 at 30掳C is the baseline. A rating of 4鈥? indicates the colour is stable under normal use. A rating below 4 means perceptible colour change within the first few wash cycles 鈥?this is the failure mode that generates customer complaints.

**ISO 105-X12: Colour Fastness to Rubbing**

This test measures whether the dye transfers to other fabrics or surfaces when the hijab is rubbed while dry or wet. For printed hijabs, dry rubbing fastness of 4 and wet rubbing fastness of 3鈥? are the standard minimum. Wet rubbing is the more demanding test: a damp white cloth rubbed against the printed surface of a poorly fixed reactive dye will pick up visible colour transfer within ten rubs.

Rubbing fastness failures are particularly damaging because they occur in visible contexts 鈥?a colourful hijab rubbing against a white shirt collar at the shoulder, for example. The customer sees the transfer immediately.

**ISO 105-B02: Colour Fastness to Artificial Light (Xenon)**

This test measures fading under light exposure equivalent to extended outdoor exposure. For everyday hijabs, a rating of 4 at 40 hours of xenon exposure is the standard reference for European markets. For sport or outdoor-use hijabs, the specification is typically higher.

Light fastness failure is slower than wash fastness failure and often goes unreported 鈥?customers assume the product has simply "aged." From a brand perspective, light fastness failure affects the visual quality of the product in stock photography and editorial content, which is shot weeks before commercial launch.

---

## Section 3: How a Factory With Systematic Quality Control Approaches Colour Fastness

Colour fastness is determined at the pre-treatment and fixation stages of production, not at the QC inspection stage. A factory that does not control these parameters cannot achieve consistent fastness ratings regardless of how carefully it inspects finished units.

**Pre-treatment chemistry for printed modal**

Modal is a regenerated cellulose fibre that requires a specific pre-treatment before reactive dye printing. The pre-treatment 鈥?typically a sodium bicarbonate or urea-based solution 鈥?performs two functions: it moderates the rate of dye absorption (preventing bleed at fine-line details) and it creates the alkaline environment needed for the reactive dye to form a covalent bond with the fibre. Without this bond, the dye sits on the surface rather than within the fibre structure, and wash fastness ratings fall below 3.

The concentration and application method of the pre-treatment are calibrated for the specific modal blend being printed. A 95% modal / 5% spandex blend behaves differently from a 100% modal base 鈥?the spandex content affects moisture absorption and therefore dye penetration. A factory that applies the same pre-treatment formulation to all modal blends is not managing this variable.

**Fixation for printed jersey (sublimation)**

Printed jersey uses sublimation dye, which bonds to the polyester structure under heat and pressure rather than through a chemical reaction with the fibre. The fixation parameters 鈥?temperature (typically 180鈥?95掳C), dwell time (20鈥?0 seconds), and pressure 鈥?determine how completely the dye migrates from the transfer paper into the polyester polymer. Under-fixation leaves dye molecules that are loosely attached to the surface and will transfer or fade rapidly. Over-fixation degrades the spandex content (spandex begins to lose elasticity above 200掳C).

A factory controlling sublimation fastness will record the temperature and dwell time for every production run and will have a calibration record for the heat press or continuous calender being used. The recorded temperature should be verified with an independent contact thermometer, not assumed from the machine's own display.

**In-line colour monitoring**

Colour delta-E is measured during the production run, not only at the end. The standard for branded hijab production is 螖E 鈮?2.0 between the approved colour reference and any unit in the production run. A reading above 螖E 2.0 during an in-line check should trigger a process pause and parameter adjustment before production continues. A factory that measures colour only at final inspection and applies no in-line correction will have a standard deviation in colour consistency that becomes visible across different production batches of the same design.

Our target and consistent first-pass yield for printed modal and printed jersey runs is 95鈥?8%, with colour delta-E tolerance of 鈮?2.0 as a hard checkpoint before any unit is released to packing.

---

## Section 4: The Specific Documentation a Brand Should Request Before Bulk

The most common mistake brands make at the sample approval stage is approving colour and drape without requesting the documentation that confirms how the sample was produced. A sample that looks correct but was produced under uncontrolled conditions 鈥?a pre-existing stock item, or a manually adjusted one-off 鈥?does not validate the factory's production capability.

The documentation that validates a sample as representative of bulk production:

**Production calibration record for the sample run**
This document should show the pre-treatment formulation, print head calibration settings, ink density curves applied, and fixation parameters (temperature, dwell time, pressure for jersey; wash time, temperature, and chemical concentrations for modal post-treatment). If this document does not exist, the sample was not produced under documented process control.

**Spectrophotometer measurement of the sample against target**
The measurement should be taken at three points on the scarf 鈥?both ends and the centre 鈥?to confirm colour consistency across the length. The delta-E reading at each point should be stated. 螖E 鈮?2.0 at all three points confirms consistent dye penetration across the full print area.

**ISO 105-C06 wash fastness test result for the fabric and dye combination**
This can be an in-house test result or a third-party laboratory report. For brands requiring third-party verification, SGS and Intertek both operate laboratories in China capable of issuing internationally recognised test certificates. A minimum rating of 4 on the specific wash programme matching the product's care label is the standard.

**GSM measurement of the base fabric**
The base fabric GSM should be measured from the production roll used for the sample, not from a separate reference sample. For printed modal, the target base weight is 60鈥?0 g/m虏, with a tolerance of 卤3 g/m虏. The finished scarf weight 鈥?after printing, trimming, and finishing 鈥?will be approximately 100鈥?20 g/m虏 depending on the trim applied. Both figures should be stated in the spec sheet.

---

## Section 5: Choosing a Manufacturer Based on Colour Consistency Standards

Colour fastness capability is not uniformly distributed across manufacturers. The question is not whether a factory has printing equipment 鈥?it is whether the factory has the process infrastructure to produce consistent colour across a production run, and consistent colour across multiple production runs separated by weeks or months.

The questions that reveal this infrastructure:

**"What is your colour delta-E specification for production runs, and how is it enforced?"**
The correct answer states a specific number (螖E 鈮?2.0 is the standard for branded production) and describes the measurement equipment (a spectrophotometer, not visual comparison) and the check frequency (every 50 metres of fabric for continuous prints, or at each panel for individual-piece printing).

**"Can you provide a wash fastness test report for printed modal and for printed jersey separately?"**
The two fabrics use different dye chemistry. A test report for modal reactive dye does not validate jersey sublimation fastness, and vice versa. A factory that produces both should have test data for both.

**"What is your pre-treatment formulation for modal, and does it vary by spandex content?"**
This question separates factories that manage pre-treatment as a variable from those that apply a standard setting to all modal. The answer should confirm that the formulation is adjusted for different blend ratios.

**"How do you handle a colour delta-E exceedance detected during an in-line check?"**
The correct answer describes a defined process: production pauses, the parameter causing the exceedance is identified and corrected, a validation print is measured before production resumes, and the out-of-specification units are quarantined. If the answer is "we adjust and continue," the factory does not have a stop-and-correct protocol.

A manufacturer that can answer these questions specifically 鈥?with reference to equipment, process records, and documented correction procedures 鈥?is operating at a level appropriate for seasonal branded production where colour consistency across batches is a commercial requirement.

---

## Section 6: Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best fabric for printed hijabs that need to hold colour after washing?**

Printed modal (95% modal, 5% spandex, 60鈥?0 g/m虏 base weight) with reactive dye achieves ISO 105-C06 wash fastness ratings of 4鈥? when correctly pre-treated and processed. Printed jersey (88% polyester, 12% spandex) with sublimation dye achieves equivalent ratings under the same standard, because the dye bonds to the polymer structure rather than sitting on the surface. Both are appropriate for premium branded production when the manufacturer controls pre-treatment chemistry, dye concentration, and fixation parameters correctly. The differentiator is not the fabric type 鈥?it is whether the manufacturer manages these variables with documented process control.

**How can brands customise colour matching in printed hijabs?**

Brands specify colour targets using Pantone references or physical fabric swatches. The manufacturer measures the produced sample against the target using a spectrophotometer; a delta-E of 鈮?2.0 between target and production is the standard for branded runs. **What documentation should buyers request from a hijab manufacturer before placing bulk?**

body:
## Why the Sampling Stage Determines Whether a Private Label Launch Succeeds

Most private label hijab brands underestimate how much of their eventual product quality is determined in the first 5鈥? days of sampling, before a single bulk unit is produced. The sample is not a preview of the product 鈥?it is the production specification. Every detail approved or overlooked at the sample stage is locked into the bulk run.

Brands that skip thorough sample evaluation to accelerate their launch timeline consistently encounter the same set of problems: colour variance between the sample and the bulk delivery, size inconsistency across units, or edge finishing that passes at a glance but fails under the scrutiny of the customer who paid for a branded product.

This guide walks through the complete production timeline for a private label printed hijab order 鈥?from the first conversation with a manufacturer through to bulk delivery 鈥?and identifies the decisions at each stage that affect the outcome.

---

## Section 1: Why Private Label Is Growing in the Modest Fashion Market

The modest fashion segment has undergone a structural shift in the past four years. Brands that previously operated as curators 鈥?buying wholesale inventory and reselling 鈥?are increasingly moving to private label production. The economics are clear: a private label brand controls its own inventory, margin, and visual identity. The operational barrier that previously made private label inaccessible to small brands 鈥?minimum order quantities, long lead times, complex manufacturing relationships 鈥?has been substantially reduced by manufacturers who have built small-batch production capability.

In the European and US markets, the DTC brands that are growing fastest in the modest fashion category are operating with inventory cycles of 60鈥?0 days and launching new colourways or designs every four to six weeks. This cadence is not compatible with the 90鈥?20 day lead times that characterised private label production a decade ago. The manufacturers who serve this segment have adapted: sampling in 5鈥? days, bulk lead times of 25鈥?5 days for standard orders, and minimum order quantities that start at 1 piece for sampling.

The brand that can move from design concept to a new colourway in the market in under 45 days has a competitive advantage over one that requires 90 days for the same cycle. The timeline discipline that makes this possible starts at the sampling stage.

---

## Section 2: What Brands Building a Private Label Hijab Line Need to Know Before Ordering

Brands entering private label hijab production for the first time consistently underestimate two things: the number of decisions that need to be made before sampling begins, and the importance of reviewing the physical sample against documented specifications rather than visual impression alone.

**Decisions required before a sample can be produced**

A manufacturer cannot produce a representative sample without a complete specification. The minimum required inputs are:

- Fabric type: printed modal or printed jersey, with the specific blend ratio (95/5 modal/spandex or 88/12 polyester/spandex)
- Print design: artwork file in AI, PSD, or high-resolution TIFF format, or a brief describing the colour palette and pattern direction for in-house design
- Colour targets: Pantone references or physical fabric swatches for the base colour and print colours
- Finished size: standard is 180脳70 cm; custom sizes 鈥?wider Gulf market dimensions (190脳80 cm), European dimensions (185脳75 cm), Malaysian dimensions (175脳65 cm), or children's sizes (120鈥?40脳55 cm) 鈥?require explicit specification
- Edge finishing: rolled hem, plain hem, lace trim, ruffle, tassel, or floral trim 鈥?each has a different production process and lead time
- Packaging: folded in tissue paper, individual poly bag, branded box 鈥?packaging specification affects the sampling lead time if branded packaging is required

Brands that provide all six inputs at the initial inquiry receive a sample faster and with fewer revision rounds than those who provide partial specifications and build the spec iteratively through the sampling process.

**The difference between a production-representative sample and a stock sample**

Some manufacturers fulfil sample requests from existing stock or from surplus units in a previous production run. These samples look correct 鈥?they may be the right fabric, the right general colour, the right size 鈥?but they are not produced under the specific process conditions that will be applied to the brand's bulk order. When the brand approves a stock sample and releases a bulk order, the bulk units are produced under different conditions than the sample, and the result frequently does not match.

A production-representative sample is produced specifically to the brand's specification, using the pre-treatment chemistry, ink density curves, fixation parameters, and edge finishing method that will be applied to the bulk order. The calibration record from the sample run is the document that confirms this. A manufacturer who cannot provide a calibration record from the sample run is either using stock samples or does not operate with documented process control.

---

## Section 3: The Complete Production Timeline 鈥?Stage by Stage

The timeline below reflects the production sequence for a printed modal or printed jersey private label hijab, starting from a complete specification brief and ending at bulk delivery ex-factory (Yiwu, China).

**Stage 1: Inquiry and specification confirmation 鈥?1鈥? working days**

The brand submits its specification brief. The manufacturer reviews it, confirms any missing inputs, and provides a quotation covering unit price, sampling cost (if any), and production lead time. For printed modal and jersey hijabs, sampling is included without additional charge for qualified wholesale buyers; shipping cost is payable by the buyer.

**Stage 2: In-house design (if required) 鈥?2鈥? working days**

If the brand does not have existing print artwork, the manufacturer's design team produces pattern options based on the brief. The brand reviews and approves digitally before physical sampling begins. This stage can run in parallel with fabric procurement if the brand can approve the design file within 24 hours.

**Stage 3: Physical sampling 鈥?5鈥? working days from artwork confirmation**

The sample is produced under documented process conditions:
- Pre-treatment chemistry applied to the base fabric (modal blend or polyester blend)
- Print head calibration and ink density curves set to the approved colour targets
- Fixation at the appropriate temperature and dwell time (sublimation for jersey: 180鈥?95掳C, 20鈥?0 seconds; reactive fixation for modal: wash-off and neutralisation process)
- Edge finishing applied using the specified method
- Colour delta-E measured at three points across the scarf (both ends and centre); target 螖E 鈮?2.0 against colour reference
- GSM measured from the production fabric: 60鈥?0 g/m虏 base, 100鈥?20 g/m虏 finished (including trim contribution)

The completed sample is dispatched by express courier. Transit time to Europe is typically 3鈥? working days; to the US, 5鈥? working days.

**Stage 4: Brand review and approval 鈥?variable, brand-controlled**

The brand reviews the physical sample against the specification. The review should cover colour (measured against the approved reference, not assessed visually), size (measured against the specified dimensions), edge finishing (inspected under consistent lighting), and wash fastness (a home wash test at 30掳C will identify major fastness failures within one cycle).

If the sample meets specification, the brand issues approval and pays the agreed deposit (typically 30% of bulk order value). If revisions are required, the manufacturer produces a revised sample; the additional sampling round adds 5鈥? working days.

**Stage 5: Bulk production 鈥?25鈥?5 working days from deposit payment**

Bulk production begins after deposit receipt. The production sequence is:
1. Fabric procurement and incoming GSM inspection (3鈥? days if fabric is not in stock)
2. Pre-treatment and print preparation (1鈥? days per colour)
3. Printing run 鈥?at a first-pass yield target of 95鈥?8%, a run of 300 units produces 285鈥?94 acceptable units on the first pass; any rejected units are reprinted within the production window
4. Post-treatment (reactive dye fixation for modal; cooling and trimming for jersey)
5. Edge finishing (rolled hem, lace attachment, tassel knotting, or embroidery 鈥?each has a different time allowance per unit)
6. Quality inspection: each unit is measured for size variance (tolerance 卤0.5 cm on length, 卤0.3 cm on width), colour consistency, and edge finishing quality
7. Packing and preparation for shipment

Peak season (August鈥揙ctober) extends bulk lead time by 5鈥?0 working days due to higher production volume across the factory.

**Stage 6: Shipment**

Ex-factory (Yiwu) by sea or air, depending on the brand's timeline and cost requirements. Standard DHL or FedEx air freight to Europe takes 5鈥? working days; to the US, 7鈥?0 working days. Sea freight is significantly lower cost but adds 20鈥?5 days depending on the destination port.

The complete timeline from specification brief to product in-hand (Europe, air freight): approximately 45鈥?5 working days for a first order including one sample revision round. For repeat orders with an approved specification, the timeline reduces to 30鈥?0 working days.

---

## Section 4: The Production Variables That Most Affect Timeline and Quality

**Artwork format and resolution**

Print artwork submitted in a low-resolution format 鈥?JPEG under 150 dpi, or a web-resolution PNG 鈥?requires conversion and interpolation before it can be used for textile printing. Conversion introduces artefacts that appear in the printed output as blurring at fine-line details or colour banding in gradient areas. Artwork submitted in AI or PSD format at a minimum of 150 dpi at print size avoids this entirely.

**Colour specification method**

Colour targets specified by name ("dusty rose," "sage green") require interpretation by the design team and are frequently misinterpreted. Pantone references, or physical fabric swatches in the target colour, allow the manufacturer to measure an exact target value and calibrate the print parameters against a known number rather than a subjective description.

**Edge finishing selection**

The edge finishing method most significantly affects the lead time beyond the fabric production stage. A rolled hem adds approximately 3鈥? minutes per unit; lace trim attachment adds 8鈥?2 minutes per unit depending on the lace width and attachment method; tassel knotting adds 15鈥?0 minutes per unit for standard fringe density. For a 300-unit order, the difference between a rolled hem and tassel fringe represents approximately 60 hours of additional labour 鈥?roughly 2 additional working days at the finishing stage.

**Order quantity and its effect on first-pass yield efficiency**

At very small quantities (under 50 units), the fixed-cost elements of a production run 鈥?pre-treatment preparation, print head calibration, fixation parameter setting 鈥?represent a higher proportion of total production time. The effective first-pass yield at quantities under 50 units is typically 90鈥?3% rather than the 95鈥?8% achievable at 300 units, because the calibration at the beginning of the run takes longer as a fraction of total units produced.

---

## Section 5: Choosing a Manufacturer Based on Their Small-Batch Capability

Not all manufacturers who claim small-batch capability have the process infrastructure to produce it consistently. The questions that reveal genuine capability:

**"What is your minimum order quantity for a new design, and is it the same for repeat colourways?"**
A manufacturer with genuine small-batch capability will offer sampling from 1 piece and will not require a minimum bulk order to activate sampling. Repeat colourways of an approved design should have the same or lower minimum than the initial design, because the print calibration data from the first run reduces the setup cost.

**"What is your sampling lead time if I provide complete artwork today?"**
The answer should be 5鈥? working days for printed modal or jersey without custom edge finishing, and 7鈥?0 working days with lace, ruffle, or tassel finishing. Lead times quoted beyond 14 days for sampling suggest either a production backlog or a workflow that does not prioritise small-batch requests.

**"Can you provide a calibration record from the sample run?"**
This document confirms the sample was produced under controlled conditions that can be replicated at bulk. A manufacturer who cannot provide this document either does not maintain process records or is providing a stock sample rather than a production-representative one.

**"What is your first-pass yield for printed modal and for printed jersey?"**
A factory targeting 95鈥?8% FPY has process control that prevents the waste and rework that drive up per-unit cost on small runs. A factory with a lower FPY will compensate by quoting a higher per-unit price or longer lead time to absorb rework.

---

## Section 6: Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best fabric for a private label hijab brand launching with small quantities?**

Printed modal (95% modal, 5% spandex, 60鈥?0 g/m虏 base fabric) is the most practical starting point for a private label brand launching with small quantities. It photographs well across a wide range of lighting conditions, has a soft hand-feel that generates positive first reviews, and reactive dye printing produces the colour accuracy needed for branded work 鈥?螖E 鈮?2.0 is achievable consistently when pre-treatment is correctly managed. Printed jersey suits brands targeting the sport or active segment. Both fabrics are available from a single-piece sample, allowing a brand to validate the full specification before committing to bulk.

**How can a brand customise a printed hijab from scratch with no existing design?**

A brand without existing artwork starts with a mood board or colour reference 鈥?Pantone numbers, physical swatches, or reference images. The factory's in-house design team produces print pattern options in AI or PSD format for brand approval. Once the design is confirmed digitally, a 1-piece physical sample is produced in 5鈥? working days. The sample covers the full specification: fabric, print, finished size (standard 180脳70 cm or any custom dimension, including children's sizes from 120脳55 cm), and edge finishing. The brand approves or requests revisions before bulk production begins.

**What should a brand check before approving a sample and releasing payment for bulk production?**

Five points should be verified on the physical sample before bulk approval: (1) Colour accuracy 鈥?request the spectrophotometer reading showing 螖E 鈮?2.0 against the colour target; (2) Fabric weight 鈥?request the GSM measurement from the production roll, target 60鈥?0 g/m虏 base for printed modal; (3) Dimensional accuracy 鈥?measure the finished scarf against the specified length and width, tolerance 卤0.5 cm; (4) Wash fastness 鈥?run a 30掳C home wash and inspect for colour change or transfer; (5) Edge finishing quality 鈥?inspect hem alignment and tension consistency under good lighting. All five should be confirmed on the physical sample before bulk payment is released.
